articles.title: A New Mexico carver, Ross Ward, spent decades building Tinkertown from carved wood and 50,000 discarded bottles; the 22-room museum opened to visitors in 1983
articles.summary: US News: Explore Tinkertown Museum, a one-of-a-kind folk-art attraction in New Mexico created by artist Ross Ward. Journey through a maze of handcrafted scenes, mechanical animations, and 50,000 glass bottles that showcase his artistic legacy.
articles.body: A childhood fascination with miniature figures eventually became one of New Mexico's most unusual folk-art attractions. In 1962, self-taught artist Ross Ward began carving small wooden figures as a hobby, initially creating scenes that could travel with him to fairs and carnivals. Over the next four decades, the hobby expanded into an elaborate handmade world at Sandia Park, where thousands of carved characters, animated displays, collections of Americana and walls made from tens of thousands of discarded glass bottles eventually became Tinkertown Museum.From carnival signs to tiny townsAccording to Spaces Archives, Ward was born in 1940 and developed his artistic skills without formal training. After working in roadside attractions, he spent years travelling with carnivals and circuses, painting banners and advertisements. At the same time, he was developing his own miniature figures. His carvings were first displayed as a travelling exhibit at county fairs and carnivals during the 1960s and 1970s, giving him a way to take his growing collection on the road. As the collection expanded, however, Ward began looking beyond the limitations of a portable display. After settling in New Mexico, he started building permanent settings for his figures, gradually transforming the travelling collection into a larger, interconnected environment. The figures were no longer simply individual carvings. He created a Western town, shops, a saloon, a hotel, a blacksmith and other scenes populated by tiny wooden inhabitants. The displays were designed to move as well as to be viewed, turning the miniature town into a kind of mechanical theatre. Visitors could also activate some of the scenes with coins, setting figures and machines into motion.The museum itself eventually became another part of Ward’s art. More than 50,000 glass bottles were incorporated into concrete walls around the building, many of them collected from roadsides, dumps and neighbours. What began as a practical use for discarded bottles developed into an architectural feature that gave Tinkertown its distinctive appearance. Ward also filled the site with discarded objects that might otherwise have been thrown away. Wagon wheels, old signs, tools, toys, agricultural equipment and other pieces of Americana became part of the surroundings. Over time, the portable miniature displays and the permanent architecture became increasingly interconnected, making the building itself part of the experience. The result was less like a conventional museum and more like a maze in which the building, collections and sculptures formed a single artwork.A museum built one piece at a timeAccording to Tinkertown Museum, the museum opened to the public in 1983 and had grown from Ross Ward’s small summer cabin into a 22-room collection of handmade displays. Its winding spaces contained an animated miniature Western town, a detailed circus, coin-operated attractions such as Otto the One-Man-Band, collections of antique tools and dolls, thousands of wedding-cake figures and the 35-foot antique sailboat Theodora R. By then, what had begun as a travelling collection had become a permanent environment that combined Ward’s carving, mechanical work, collecting and construction. He spent much of his adult life carving, painting, collecting and constructing, rather than producing a single finished work for a gallery. The museum therefore became as much a record of his interests as a display of his craftsmanship. His attraction to the Old West, travelling shows and everyday American life was reflected repeatedly in both the carved scenes and the objects surrounding them. The building’s handmade character also placed Tinkertown within the tradition of self-taught and outsider folk-art environments, where artists transformed private properties into immersive spaces rather than creating isolated artworks.Keeping Ward's world aliveThe Spaces archive also notes that Ward continued developing Tinkertown for decades, but his health eventually limited his work. He was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease in 1998 and died in 2002, leaving behind the museum he had spent much of his life constructing. His wife, Carla, and other family members continued caring for the attraction and keeping it open to visitors. According to the museum, the attraction grew from welcoming 943 visitors in 1983 to attracting around 25,000 visitors each season. In 2026, the family converted the museum into a public nonprofit, a step intended to support the long-term preservation of its buildings, artwork and Ward’s wider artistic legacy. More than six decades after Ward began carving his miniature figures, Tinkertown remains a testament to what can emerge from a lifelong hobby. Its maze of handmade scenes, collections and bottle walls preserves not only Ward’s craftsmanship but also his vision of creating an environment entirely on his own terms.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the 1940s, Nevada’s six-week divorce law turned a 1,627-acre ranch into a refuge for women seeking quick divorces; after 155 years in private hands, it is becoming the state’s 28th park
articles.summary: US News: For decades, a sprawling stretch of land along Nevada’s Carson River had a rather unusual place in the state’s history. In the 1940s and 1950s, part o.
articles.body: For decades, a sprawling stretch of land along Nevada’s Carson River had a rather unusual place in the state’s history. In the 1940s and 1950s, part of the property operated as a “divorce ranch”, offering a temporary refuge for people seeking to end their marriages under Nevada’s famously lenient divorce laws.Now, more than 70 years later, the same 1,627-acre landscape is beginning a completely different chapter. After more than 155 years in private ownership, the Lower Carson Ranch has been transferred to Nevada State Parks and is becoming the state’s 28th state park.The property, located near Dayton in Lyon County, stretches along approximately 4.5 miles of the lower Carson River. Its transition from a privately held ranch and historic divorce destination into protected public land is expected to preserve important wildlife habitat while eventually giving visitors access to a landscape that has remained largely private for generations.The ranch where people came to end their marriagesDuring the 1940s, Nevada had developed a reputation as one of the easiest places in the United States to obtain a divorce. The state required people seeking a divorce to establish residency for only six weeks before they could pursue the legal process.That relatively short residency requirement created a unique industry. People from across the country travelled to Nevada, often staying at specialised ranches while waiting to meet the residency requirement and complete their divorces.Part of the Lower Carson Ranch became one of these so-called divorce ranches during the 1940s. The properties offered visitors a place to stay while they waited out the required period, turning divorce into an unusual form of tourism in the state.The ranch was not simply a place where people passed through. It became part of a broader Nevada phenomenon in which wealthy and middle-class Americans could escape the restrictions and lengthy legal processes surrounding divorce in their home states.A 155-year private legacy enters a new chapterThe Lower Carson Ranch had remained in private hands for more than 150 years before its transfer to Nevada State Parks. Its new status means the landscape will eventually become accessible to the public while protecting its river corridor and surrounding habitat. The property contains important riparian areas along the Carson River, providing habitat for fish and wildlife. Conservation of the river corridor was a major part of the effort to protect the land.The landscape lies within the traditional homelands of the Numu, or Northern Paiute, and Wá∙šiw, or Washoe, peoples. Its history also includes Indigenous stewardship, emigrant travel routes and generations of ranching.The land was formally conveyed to Nevada State Parks by the Western Rivers Conservancy in July 2026. The conservation organisation worked to protect the property and transfer it to the state, ensuring that its riverfront habitat would be permanently conserved.Interestingly, Nevada’s newest state park does not yet have an official name. Nevada State Parks launched a public process to choose one, inviting people to vote on three proposed names: Crossroads Canyon State Park, Heritage Canyon State Park and River’s Edge State Park.Each name was intended to reflect a different aspect of the property:Crossroads Canyon State Park refers to the movement of people and cultures through the region, while also acknowledging the landscape’s canyon setting and its unusual history as a divorce ranch.Heritage Canyon State Park focuses on the area's Indigenous, emigrant and ranching history.River’s Edge State Park highlights the Carson River and the property's future as a place for conservation and recreation.Voting took place from August 1 to August 14, 2026, with the official name expected to be announced in fall 2026.Although the property has officially entered Nevada’s state park system, visitors will have to wait before they can freely explore the entire 1,627 acres. Nevada State Parks currently says public access is limited to Fort Churchill Road, as the new park still needs development before it can fully welcome visitors. That means the transformation is still in its early stages. Over time, however, the former private ranch is expected to offer opportunities for recreation, conservation and education along the Carson River.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: How to avoid rental disputes: Delhi Police plans awareness session for Northeast tenants
articles.summary: News News: Delhi Police will hold an awareness programme next week to help people from the Northeast, including Gorkhas from Darjeeling and Ladakhis, better unde.
articles.body: Delhi Police will hold an awareness programme next week to help people from the Northeast, including Gorkhas from Darjeeling and Ladakhis, better understand issues related to rental agreements and disputes over security deposits with landlords.The programme, organised by the Special Police Unit for North-East Region (SPUNER), will be held at 3.30 pm on September 1 at the SPUNER office in Nanak Pura, Moti Bagh, according to news agency PTI.The initiative will focus on helping tenants understand their rights and responsibilities and avoid disagreements with landlords, particularly over the payment, refund and deduction of security deposits.Focus on rent agreements and proof of paymentAccording to the circular released, the awareness programme will cover the importance of having written rent agreements, understanding issues related to security deposit refunds and deductions, tenant responsibilities and preserving documents and proof of payments."The Awareness Programme will focus on sensitising the North-Eastern people regarding written rent agreements, security deposit/refund/deductions, tenant responsibilities and preservation of relevant documents/proof of payment," the circular said.Tenants will also be advised to safely keep rent agreements, payment records and other relevant documents that could be required in the event of a dispute with a landlord.Advisory to be circulated across Northeast communityThe police plan to circulate the advisory widely among members of the Northeast community living in Delhi with the help of Delhi Police Northeast Region personnel, students and community leaders.The programme will also include Gorkhas from Darjeeling and Ladakhis, according to the circular."Therefore, DPNErs & students and community leaders are hereby requested to attend the aforesaid awareness programme and facilitate wide dissemination of the above advisory amongst the North-Eastern community in Delhi," it articles.title: Kabul, Kashmir, Mumbai, Pahalgam: Hafiz Saeed’s deadly four-decade terror trail
articles.summary: Pakistan News: The legal case against Lashkar-e-Taiba founder Hafiz Muhammad Saeed has acquired a fresh dimension in India. In July 2026, the National Investigation .
articles.body: The legal case against Lashkar-e-Taiba founder Hafiz Muhammad Saeed has acquired a fresh dimension in India. In July 2026, the National Investigation Agency named Saeed in a supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam terror attack case, charging him in his individual capacity and as the founder and chief of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and its active proxy, The Resistance Front (TRF). The NIA mentioned a cross-border conspiracy behind the April 22, 2025 attack, which killed 26 civilians. A special NIA court subsequently issued a non-bailable warrant against Saeed.The development came as Mumbai Police separately began proceedings for a trial in absentia against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks. The proclamation covers Saeed, LeT operations chief Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, Sajid Mir, Abu Alqama, Asim alias Abu Qahafa and Major Abdur Rehman Pasha. The police have also approached the Union home ministry to facilitate service of the proclamation orders through Interpol.The two cases, separated by 17 years, bring together different phases of LeT's history. One concerns an attack in Kashmir, the region that became the organisation's principal battlefield in the 1990s. The other concerns the Mumbai attacks, which demonstrated how far LeT's operational reach had expanded beyond the Kashmir insurgency.But LeT did not begin in Kashmir, nor did Hafiz Saeed first emerge as a militant leader there. The organisation's institutional roots can be traced to the Afghan jihad of the 1980s, when Pakistan became a major centre for the mobilisation, training and movement of Islamist fighters.The Afghan war that created LeT's foundationsThe Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 created an environment in which Islamist networks from Pakistan and other parts of the Muslim world expanded rapidly. Among the prominent figures associated with this mobilisation was Palestinian scholar Abdullah Azzam, who helped organise foreign volunteers for the Afghan jihad and promoted the idea of jihad as a broader obligation extending beyond a single battlefield.It was in this environment that Azzam worked with Hafiz Saeed, a Pakistani Sunni scholar who had studied in Saudi Arabia. According to Bruce Riedel's Deadly Embrace: Pakistan, America, and the Future of the Global Jihad, the two were involved in establishing Markaz-ud-Dawa-wal-Irshad (MDI), a religious organisation that combined missionary activity with support for jihad. MDI developed training infrastructure in Afghanistan, including in Kunar province, where recruits could gain battlefield experience. Riedel also records links between the organisation and Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI).Lashkar-e-Taiba subsequently emerged as the military wing associated with this network. The US state department describes LeT as having formed in the late 1980s as the militant wing of MDI, an organisation originally established in opposition to the Soviet presence in Afghanistan. The Australian government dates LeT's formation as a military organisation to 1989.The exact formation date therefore varies depending on whether the establishment of MDI, the creation of its military wing or the later formalisation of LeT is being referred to. What is clearer is the sequence: the Afghan jihad provided the organisation's early ideological, human and training infrastructure, while the end of the Soviet war opened the way for that infrastructure to be redirected towards other conflicts.Why Lashkar-e-Taiba was establishedLeT's early purpose was shaped by two connected objectives: participation in the Afghan jihad and preparation for jihad in Kashmir and India. Riedel describes MDI's objective as applying the experience of the Afghan war to Kashmir and India, including training Kashmiris alongside Afghan mujahideen so they could gain combat experience.The changing situation in Afghanistan accelerated that transition. The Soviet withdrawal meant that the battlefield that had brought together thousands of militants was no longer the same. At the same time, violence in Jammu and Kashmir was rising sharply.The Australian government's account of LeT's history says the organisation was originally formed to wage militant jihad against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan and shifted its focus to the insurgency in Indian-administered Kashmir during the 1990s after Soviet troops withdrew. It identifies the organisation's stated objective as uniting Kashmir with Pakistan, while noting that its broader ideological objectives extended beyond Kashmir.Kashmir thus became the next major theatre in which the organisation could deploy the personnel, training and networks developed during the Afghan war.From Kunar to KashmirThe shift towards Kashmir coincided with the rapid growth of the insurgency there. Riedel records that incidents of violence in Kashmir rose from 390 in 1988 to 2,100 in 1989 and nearly 4,000 in 1990. Against this backdrop, Saeed's organisation began establishing infrastructure in and around Kashmir while maintaining training facilities in Pakistan and Afghanistan.LeT's emergence also coincided with changes among the various groups fighting in Kashmir. The Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front advocated an independent Kashmir, while Pakistan's security establishment increasingly favoured groups committed to the territory's integration with Pakistan. Riedel describes efforts to strengthen pro-Pakistan organisations and isolate the JKLF, which was regarded as too independent. Hizbul Mujahideen became a major pro-Pakistan militant force, while LeT developed its own network and capabilities.By the 1990s, Kashmir had become LeT's principal operational theatre. The organisation developed training and recruitment networks and directed fighters towards attacks on Indian security forces. Stephen Tankel, in Lashkar-e-Taiba: From 9/11 to Mumbai, describes Kashmir as the group's primary objective even as its connections to the wider global jihadist movement expanded.This distinction is important. LeT developed relationships with al Qaida and other jihadist groups, but its core focus remained India and Kashmir. Riedel similarly distinguishes between the different objectives of the groups operating in the region, noting that the Afghan Taliban remained primarily focused on Afghanistan while LeT concentrated on South Asia. At the operational level, however, their cooperation increased.Hafiz Saeed - From cleric to terroristSaeed's prominence grew alongside the institutional development of MDI and LeT. He was not simply the leader of an armed organisation. The network around him combined religious propagation, education, charity and terror activity.Riedel describes Saeed as a prominent Pakistani Sunni scholar who worked with Azzam in developing MDI. The organisation's combination of religious activity and military infrastructure provided the foundation for the later growth of LeT.LeT's recruitment base was also closely connected to Pakistani society. Riedel writes that the organisation was predominantly Punjabi and recruited from many of the same communities and neighbourhoods as the Pakistani army and ISI. He also describes LeT camps located near army bases and the involvement of retired military personnel in training fighters.The nature and extent of state support for LeT has remained a matter of dispute, but the organisation's relationship with Pakistan's security establishment became an important part of its history. The United Nations Security Council identifies LeT as a Pakistan-based organisation and records its links with al Qaida and the Taliban, as well as its use of Jamaat-ud-Dawa for financial, logistical and infrastructural support.LeT survives Pakistani ban after 9/11The September 11, 2001 attacks changed the environment for militant organisations operating from Pakistan. The United States designated LeT as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation in December 2001, while Pakistan banned the group in January 2002.The ban, however, did not eliminate the network. The US state department says Saeed subsequently changed the group's name to Jamaat-ud-Dawa and expanded its humanitarian activities, while continuing to disseminate its message through JuD's media outlets.Riedel similarly writes that although LeT was formally banned, it continued to operate and Saeed remained in charge. He describes the organisation's large facility at Muridke near Lahore, which included schools, dormitories, a garment factory, an iron foundry and a mosque.This structure helped the network maintain a presence beyond its armed operations. Religious institutions, charitable activity, fundraising and recruitment provided a broader organisational base that could continue even when the LeT name itself faced restrictions.The United Nations says LeT used JuD as a front through which it provided financial, logistical and infrastructural support for terrorist activity. It also records that an al Qaida operative, Abu Zubaydah, was captured in 2002 in a LeT safe house in Faisalabad, illustrating the organisation's connections to the wider jihadist network.From Kashmir insurgency to MumbaiThe years after 2001 saw LeT's operational reach extend beyond the traditional Kashmir battlefield. The United Nations records that the organisation conducted terrorist operations against military and civilian targets from the 1990s onwards, including attacks in New Delhi and Mumbai and the December 2001 Parliament attack, in which Jaish-e-Mohammed was also involved.The 2008 Mumbai attacks represented the most significant expansion of that reach. Ten attackers carried out coordinated assaults across Mumbai between November 26 and 29, killing 166 people. The attack targeted several locations, including the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi-Trident and Nariman House.The operation also demonstrated the organisational depth behind LeT's attacks. Riedel's account details the role of David Coleman Headley, who joined LeT in Pakistan and later conducted reconnaissance in Mumbai. Between 2005 and 2008, Headley travelled repeatedly to India, studying targets, recording locations and reporting back to LeT.The Mumbai operation therefore represented more than an extension of the Kashmir insurgency. It demonstrated the organisation's ability to plan and execute a complex attack far from its traditional theatre while drawing on personnel, training and logistical networks developed over decades.Why Afghanistan remained part of the networkThe shift to Kashmir did not end LeT's involvement in Afghanistan. Instead, the two theatres became connected through overlapping militant networks.Riedel wrote that LeT became increasingly active in Afghanistan, including operations against Indian interests and clashes with Nato forces. He also described growing operational links between LeT and the Afghan Taliban, particularly the Haqqani network.The United Nations likewise records LeT's activity in Afghanistan and its links with al Qaida and the Taliban. The Australian government has documented LeT's continued presence in Afghanistan and reported that the UN estimated the group had close to 1,000 members operating there in May 2020.Afghanistan therefore remained an important part of LeT's network even after Kashmir became its main operational focus. The relationships, training environments and infrastructure developed during the Afghan jihad continued to provide connections to other militant organisations.Saeed's legal history and the Pahalgam caseSaeed's subsequent legal history illustrates the difference between Pakistan's formal action against LeT and the organisation's continued existence through associated structures.Pakistan arrested Saeed in 2019 on terrorism-financing charges. He was convicted in several cases and received additional sentences in subsequent proceedings. The UN Security Council's current sanctions information says Saeed is in Pakistani custody serving a cumulative 78-year sentence following convictions in seven terrorism-financing cases.India, meanwhile, has continued to pursue him over alleged involvement in major terror attacks attributed to LeT.The latest development is the NIA's supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam case. The agency has named Saeed both individually and as the chief of LeT and TRF, alleging that he was part of the wider conspiracy behind the April 2025 attack.The subsequent non-bailable warrant followed the NIA's request for Saeed's arrest and custodial interrogation. Meanwhile, Mumbai Police has begun the process for an in-absentia trial against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 26/11 case.From Afghan jihad to PahalgamLashkar-e-Taiba's four-decade history can be traced through a sequence of changing battlefields and organisational forms. Its foundations were laid during the Afghan jihad, when Hafiz Saeed and Abdullah Azzam helped build MDI and the networks around it. After the Soviet withdrawal, the organisation redirected much of its experience and infrastructure towards Kashmir, where it became a major Pakistan-based militant group.The 2002 ban did not erase the network. It adapted through Jamaat-ud-Dawa and other associated structures, while maintaining religious, charitable and recruitment networks across Pakistan. Its links with militant groups operating in Afghanistan also survived, even as India and Kashmir remained its central focus.The Mumbai attacks showed how far that network could project violence beyond Kashmir. The Pahalgam investigation has now brought the story back to the same region where LeT established much of its early operational identity.The latest legal proceedings against Saeed therefore sit at the end of a history that began not in Mumbai or Pahalgam, but in the Afghan jihad of the 1980s.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Gang’s name similar to someone in UP’: Akhilesh Yadav’s swipe at Yogi Adityanath over Ankit Balyan murder
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav on Sunday took a swipe at Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath over the fatal shootin.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav on Sunday took a swipe at Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath over the fatal shooting of singer Ankit Balyan, stating that the gang allegedly behind the murder has a name that bears a “striking resemblance” to a “prominent figure” in the state."The bullets didn't just strike an innocent youth from our state; they also hit the law and order in the Kotwali area of UP," Akhilesh Yadav wrote in Hindi on X, referring to the location of the murder."The chief minister kept claiming that mafia and criminals have left Uttar Pradesh; but here, the opposite has happened—gangsters and thugs from other states have come to UP, firing dozens of rounds and committing murders," he added.The SP supremo was referring to speculation that the Gogi gang, which operates primarily across Delhi and Haryana, was behind Ankit Balyan's murder."Their gang's name also bears a striking resemblance to that of some prominent figure in UP. What is this connection called? The killers are brazen and their morale is sky-high because they feel a sense of belonging to the corrupt rule of the UP BJP government, which shields those of its own kind in power and corrupts the police through fake encounters," Akhilesh Yadav stated.The former chief minister's post was a direct attack on Yogi Adityanath's projection as a leader tough on law and order. The ruling BJP will seek a third consecutive term when Uttar Pradesh goes to polls early next year.Ankit Balyan, a 32-year-old singer and YouTuber from Haryana, was shot dead by four armed assailants outside a gym in Shamli's Kotwali area on August 26. Preliminary information suggested that around 18 rounds were fired at him in the point-blank attack.Police are examining a possible gang-war angle after a social media post by Bholu Shahpuriya, who is purportedly linked to the Gogi gang, claimed responsibility for the killing. The post alleged that Ankit Balyan had been supporting the gang's "enemies" and had made a song about the killing of gangster Jitender Mann, alias Gogi. It also warned that those supporting the gang's rivals would meet a "similar fate."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Himachal identifies 67 vulnerable glacial lakes, early warning systems planned for 4
articles.summary: SHIMLA: Himachal Pradesh has identified 67 vulnerable glacial lakes, including several in remote, high-altitude areas, and is working to establish ear.
articles.body: SHIMLA: Himachal Pradesh has identified 67 vulnerable glacial lakes, including several in remote, high-altitude areas, and is working to establish early warning systems for four of the most vulnerable lakes in Kinnaur and Lahaul-Spiti, Special Secretary, Disaster Management, Pushpinder Rana, said on Saturday.The state is monitoring the identified lakes using satellite imagery and other scientific data to detect changes that could heighten the risk of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs).It is also exploring technical solutions to install sensors and transmit real-time data from remote locations where conventional communication networks are unavailable.Rana told news agency ANI that the identification of a large number of vulnerable glacial lakes was a cause for concern, especially as recent disasters in the Himalayas have shown that major incidents can occur without conventional warning signs such as heavy rainfall."Number bada hai, chinta ka vishay toh hai hi (The figure is huge, it's a matter of concern). At the State Centre for Climate Change, we have identified 67 such lakes which are above 10 hectares in area. We are analysing them through satellite and other data to see whether any such situation is developing in them," he said.Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) occur when water stored in or around a glacial lake is suddenly released, sending large volumes of water downstream.These events can trigger flash floods, damage infrastructure and pose a serious threat to settlements in downstream valleys.Rana said recent incidents in the Himalayan region had highlighted the difficulty of predicting such events solely on the basis of rainfall forecasts.He said the state was therefore seeking technological solutions that could allow vulnerable lakes to be monitored continuously, particularly those situated in inaccessible terrain."Until we find an innovative way to move forward on this, we will not be able to take effective steps regarding them," Rana said.Rana said Himachal Pradesh had submitted a proposal to the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) to establish early warning systems for vulnerable glacial lakes.He said work had been taken up on four lakes in Kinnaur and Lahaul-Spiti under the National Landslide Mitigation Programme, with a focus on strengthening monitoring and early warning capabilities.The lakes include Parchu Lake and vulnerable locations in the Sangla-Kinnaur region, besides sites in Lahaul-Spiti.The proposed systems are intended to detect potentially dangerous changes in lake conditions and communicate warnings to authorities and downstream populations.However, Rana said installation of such systems at high-altitude locations remained a major technological challenge."The early warning system is a technical challenge. The problem is that these locations are in very remote areas where there is no network connectivity. Where will the sensors be installed, how will they be installed and how will the data be transferred? These are the challenges," he said.The state is working with the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) to develop technological solutions to address these challenges.Rana said the state would begin installing an early warning system at Dipang Ghat once it receives final approval from the NDMA.Alongside early warning systems, the government is undertaking High Flood Level (HFL) marking in downstream areas that could potentially be affected by a sudden release of water."The High Flood Level marking in the downstream areas that could be affected is also being taken up at Dipang Ghat. The process is underway," Rana said.Rana said regular monitoring and community awareness would form an important part of the preparedness strategy around vulnerable lakes."The idea is that we will move forward towards an early warning system. The High Flood Level marking and regular monitoring will also be deployed at such locations," he said.The state's approach is also linked to scientific studies of Himalayan glaciers and glacial lakes using satellite-based observations.Experts studying the Himalayas have increasingly used remote sensing and satellite imagery to track changes in glaciers and glacial lakes, particularly in high-altitude areas that are difficult or hazardous to access on the ground.Satellite data allow researchers to compare changes in glacier extent and lake formation across different Himalayan basins over time. Studies in Himachal Pradesh have examined basins such as the Sutlej and Spiti, documenting changes in glacier area as well as the number and size of glacial lakes.The availability of higher-resolution satellite imagery has further improved the detection of smaller water bodies and enabled more precise monitoring of changes in their extent.Such scientific monitoring is important because an increase in the number or size of glacial lakes, changes in surrounding glaciers, unstable moraine dams and other physical changes can indicate evolving risks, although individual lakes require site-specific assessment before being classified as an imminent GLOF threat.Rana said satellite data would therefore remain an important component of the state's monitoring strategy.Rana said GLOF risks could not be addressed by Himachal Pradesh or India in isolation because the Himalayan river systems and glacial landscapes extend across international boundaries."There are around 1,000 such lakes within the Indian side of the border, and to understand what is happening and how it is happening, we definitely need international knowledge and exchange," he said.He stressed the importance of sharing information about developments in high-altitude areas and upstream river systems, particularly where changes could have consequences for downstream populations.The issue assumes added importance for Himachal Pradesh because several major river systems originate in or pass through high-altitude Himalayan terrain.Rana said the state was also strengthening its broader disaster information and response mechanism.The emergency helpline 1077 is available to report disasters and potential hazards, while Emergency Response Centres at both the district and state levels operate round the clock.He said information received from different sources, including the India Meteorological Department, is assessed and verified before authorities take action.As Himachal Pradesh faces growing risks from GLOFs, flash floods, cloudbursts, landslides and other climate- and weather-related hazards, officials say a combination of satellite surveillance, scientific assessments, ground-level monitoring, early warning systems, HFL mapping and rapid emergency response will be crucial to reducing risks in vulnerable Himalayan valleys.(With agency inputs)Stay updated with the latest Shimla news. articles.title: Bangalore based 5-year-old visually impaired girl learning to walk with a cane wins 3.5 million views: Her family was once told it was ‘karma’; today, she is fighting for inclusion and independence
articles.summary: The internet came across Aeny’s story through a video posted on her Instagram account. In the clip, 5-year-old Aeny is learning to walk with a cane, t.
articles.body: The internet came across Aeny’s story through a video posted on her Instagram account. In the clip, 5-year-old Aeny is learning to walk with a cane, taking careful steps as her mother, Lopamudra Kar, guides her from a distance.Aeny moves forward, feeling her way with the cane. There are moments when she stumbles and pauses, but she keeps going. It is a simple moment between a mother and her five-year-old daughter. But for Lopamudra, it represents something much bigger, the journey of teaching Aeny not to see her visual impairment as a limit to the life she can lead.The clip has garnered over 3.5 million views on Instagram. Everyone who saw the clip couldn’t stop praising Aeny’s confidence, determination and her mother’s courage. However, those steps are a part of a much larger journey for Aeny and her family- one shaped by curiosity, independence, inclusion and her determination to explore the world around her.More than a cane: Aeny is learning, exploring and finding her own wayAeny’s days are filled with the things that make up any energetic five-year-old’s childhood- school, play, travel, learning and exploring. Along the way, she is also learning Braille, piano and abacus, cycling and practising karate. At four-and-a-half, she earned an orange belt in karate.For her parents, JyotiRanjan Mishra and Lopamudra, both IT professionals in Bengaluru, these are not extraordinary activities. They are simply opportunities they want their daughter to have.“Aeny’s day is much like any other child’s- school, learning, play in the park and lots of energy,” Lopamudra told. “What makes her journey special is not that she does everything differently, but that she continues to find her own way of doing things.”‘It took us months to accept that she couldn’t see’“As parents, it was extremely difficult to hear that our child couldn’t see. It took us months to accept the fact that she was visually impaired.” For Lopamudra, accepting Aeny’s visual impairment brought fear, grief and a question: What will my child’s future look like?“As they say, grief comes in waves. There are still days when I feel extremely low just thinking that my amazing girl may never see us.”But alongside that grief came support. Lopamudra’s parents eventually moved in with the family to help raise Aeny. Her father became one of the most important people in the little girl’s world. “He became her best friend,” Lopamudra said.For Lopamudra, having her parents beside her made a difficult phase a little more manageable. Her father would take Aeny to the park, talk to her, describe the world around her and encourage her to explore. Their presence also meant that Lopamudra could continue working while knowing that Aeny was surrounded by people she trusted.There were also strangers who offered prayers and good wishes when they learnt about Aeny. “Every prayer counts,” Lopamudra said. But not every comment was comforting.‘People told me it was because of karma’In the early years, when Lopamudra was still trying to understand what had happened to her daughter, some people told her that Aeny’s visual impairment was the result of “karma”- something she or her parents had supposedly done in a previous life.Others suggested visiting temples, performing pujas or following particular rituals to change the situation. For a frightened mother searching desperately for answers, such suggestions were difficult to dismiss. “I listened to people. I visited temples, performed pujas and tried different things for almost two years,” she said.It was not, she explained, because she wanted to blame anyone. It was because Aeny was her child and, at that point, Lopamudra was willing to try anything she believed might help.Eventually, however, her thinking changedShe realised that looking for a reason to explain Aeny’s disability was taking her away from the question that mattered more: what could she do to help her daughter build a fulfilling and independent life? “Aeny didn't need guilt, pity or explanations about why this had happened. She needed support, education, accessibility and people who believed in her,” Lopamudra said. “That was a turning point for me. I stopped asking, ‘Why did this happen to my child?’ and started asking, ‘What can I do to make sure my child gets the best possible life?’”That shift is visible in the way Aeny’s childhood has unfolded.She is learning Braille and independent living skills, attends activities designed to build confidence and independence, and enjoys cycling. She is learning piano and abacus and participates in events related to STEM. Karate has become another part of her journey. At just four-and-a-half, she earned an orange belt. For Aeny, these activities are not framed as limitations she must overcome. They are simply things she enjoys learning.As part of that effort to help Aeny become more independent, the family has also found support in Vividha Trust in Bengaluru. The organisation has been helping her learn Braille and develop independent living skills- tools that Lopamudra sees as important not just for Aeny’s education today, but for the independence she will need as she grows.Her mother says the family wants her to experience the world rather than grow up believing that disability should determine what she can or cannot attempt.Bengaluru gave her support- but inclusion remains a struggleLiving in a Tier 1 city has given Aeny access to therapies, support networks, inclusive events and people who have helped the family navigate unfamiliar territory.But when asked if the city is genuinely accessible and inclusive for Aeny, Lopamudra says she wouldn’t call it so. As the mother of a specially-abled child, Lopamudra says Bengaluru is still far from being genuinely accessible and inclusive for children with disabilities.The biggest challenge came when the family began looking for a school. Lopamudra recalls approaching more than 15 primary schools in Bengaluru, including several well-known institutions, but was unable to secure admission for Aeny. In some cases, she says, admission was offered only on the condition that the family arrange a shadow teacher.For a child at the LKG level, she says, the financial burden can also be significant, with the family spending around Rs 3.2 lakh a year. Her concern is not simply about getting Aeny into a classroom. It is about finding a school that can support her as she grows. “No school has accessible devices for special-needs children,” she said, adding that she worries about what the future will look like as Aeny moves into higher classes.The concerns come against the backdrop of India’s Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. Section 16 says educational institutions funded or recognised by the government and local authorities should provide inclusive education, including non-discriminatory admission, accessible facilities, reasonable accommodation and necessary individualised support.For Lopamudra, the issue goes beyond Aeny. She worries about the many children with disabilities who have the ability and potential to learn but continue to struggle to find schools that are willing and equipped to include them. A child’s visual impairment, she believes, should not become a reason to narrow their educational opportunities. What families need is not simply admission, but schools that have the accessible learning tools, trained support and understanding needed to help children participate and progress alongside their peers.For families like Aeny’s, however, the challenge is turning those principles into everyday reality. Lopamudra says there are many bright children with disabilities who continue to struggle to find schools equipped to meet their needs. “I am really worried about better schooling for her as she grows,” she said. “She is a really intelligent girl and the right path is required for her future.”‘Our children don’t need sympathy’If there is one thing Lopamudra wants other parents to know, it is that a diagnosis should never become a child's identity. “Never let a diagnosis define your child’s dreams or their future,” she said. The journey, she acknowledges, can come with judgement, uncertainty and moments when parents question whether they are doing enough.Her advice is to notice the small victories.“Celebrate every small achievement, because what may seem like a small step to others can be a huge victory for your child,” she said. Most importantly, she wants children with disabilities to be given opportunities to become independent rather than being constantly protected or pitied. “Just believe in your child, give them opportunities to be independent, and never stop advocating for their right to be included,” she said.And perhaps that is the heart of Aeny’s story. She is not extraordinary because she is visually impaired. Nor does she need to be described only through what she cannot see. She is five. She is learning, travelling, cycling, practising karate, discovering music, asking questions and exploring the world around her.Her parents are simply asking that the world make room for her- not as an exception, not as an object of sympathy, but as a child who deserves the same chance to discover how far she can go. As Aeny’s mother puts it, “Our children don't need sympathy. They need acceptance, accessibility, equal opportunities and the freedom to show the world what they can do.”Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: In 2013, Florida’s Tortuga Music Festival began restoring dunes with sea oats; 13 years later, fans and volunteers have planted 33,000+ on Fort Lauderdale Beach
articles.summary: US News: Music fans and environmental volunteers have planted more than 33,000 sea oats along Fort Lauderdale Beach over the past 13 years, turning an annual m.
articles.body: Music fans and environmental volunteers have planted more than 33,000 sea oats along Fort Lauderdale Beach over the past 13 years, turning an annual music festival into one of South Florida’s longest-running coastal restoration projects. The dune restoration effort began in 2013 alongside the first Tortuga Music Festival, an event created in partnership with the Rock The Ocean Foundation to raise money and awareness for marine conservation. Information published on the organisation’s official website confirms that volunteer groups and festivalgoers have planted native vegetation along the shoreline every year since the festival began. What started as a small local environmental project has grown into a long-term effort to strengthen sand dunes along busy parts of Fort Lauderdale’s barrier island.Rebuilding coastal defences with sea oatsSea oats, scientifically known as Uniola paniculata, are one of the main plants that help form sand dunes along the south-eastern coast of the United States. These tough perennial grasses have large underground root and rhizome systems that extend deep into the sand, helping hold loose grains in place and preventing them from being carried away by wind and waves. When wind moves across the beach, the tall leaves of sea oats catch blowing sand. The sand then builds up around the base of the plants. As more sand collects, the grass grows higher, creating a natural cycle that slowly builds and strengthens the dune. Coastal scientists and Florida environmental officials consider sand dunes the first major line of defence against Atlantic storms. Healthy dunes absorb some of the force of waves, high tides and storm surges, helping protect roads, buildings and homes from flooding and erosion. In busy urban beach areas such as Fort Lauderdale, heavy foot traffic and development can damage natural dunes. Bare dunes can quickly break apart when large waves reach the shore, leaving inland areas more exposed. By planting tens of thousands of sea oats over 13 years, the project has helped rebuild natural barriers along important sections of the public beach.Bringing music fans into conservationA major part of the environmental programme takes place at Conservation Village, an educational area set up at the festival each year. Information from the foundation shows that the site brings together dozens of non-profit ocean conservation groups, researchers and environmental organisations. Instead of asking festivalgoers to support conservation only through donations, organisers include hands-on environmental work as part of the event. Visitors can join guided planting sessions on the beach near the festival stages, placing sea oat plants in selected restoration areas with help from coastal resource managers. The programme gives festivalgoers a chance to meet marine scientists, learn about threats facing the oceans and take part in real restoration work before returning to the music. Money raised through Tortuga Music Festival ticket sales and corporate sponsorships supports marine conservation programmes run by Rock The Ocean around the world. The foundation focuses on five main areas: sea turtle conservation, shark protection, coral reef restoration, marine mammal protection and efforts to reduce plastic pollution.Protecting sea turtle nesting beachesThe restored dunes do more than protect the coast from storms. They also provide important habitat for wildlife, especially nesting sea turtles. Broward County’s beaches are important nesting areas for loggerhead, green and leatherback sea turtles from April through October each year. Female sea turtles use raised, plant-covered dunes to lay their eggs safely above the high-tide line. When hatchlings emerge at night, they normally follow natural light from the horizon to find their way towards the sea. On developed coastlines, artificial light from street lamps, hotels and other buildings can confuse young turtles. Instead of moving towards the ocean, they may head towards roads, buildings or drainage areas. Thick vegetation on sand dunes can provide both a physical and visual barrier, reducing the amount of artificial light reaching nesting areas and helping hatchlings move towards the natural horizon. The more than 33,000 sea oats planted since 2013 have created a tall, dense plant barrier along important sections of Fort Lauderdale Beach. This supports local wildlife officials as they work to protect vulnerable turtle nests.A model for greener festivalsThe continuing dune restoration project at Fort Lauderdale Beach shows how large public events can include environmental work as part of their operations. Outdoor festivals are often criticised for producing waste, using large amounts of energy and putting pressure on the places where they are held. By making habitat restoration part of the festival programme, Rock The Ocean and Tortuga Music Festival organisers have shown that major events can also create lasting environmental benefits for the communities that host them. Local coastal management teams monitor the restored dune areas throughout the year. They track how many plants survive and how much the dunes grow. Post-storm checks have found that beach sections supported by established sea oat root systems lose less sand during tropical weather than areas without the plants. As organisers prepare for future festival seasons, they plan to continue the annual planting programme with coastal partners and expand vegetation across other vulnerable sections of the Fort Lauderdale shoreline.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Istanbul to host first committee meeting of Turkey-Saudi-Pakistan defence alliance: Report
articles.summary: International News: Top officials from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will gather in Istanbul on Monday for the first committee meeting under the joint defence accord .
articles.body: Top officials from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will gather in Istanbul on Monday for the first committee meeting under the joint defence accord the three countries signed earlier this month, a Turkish foreign ministry source told Reuters.Foreign and defence ministers, along with the chiefs of staff of the three countries, are expected to attend the meeting.The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on August 7, brought together the three Sunni Muslim-majority US allies amid the Iran war and wider regional conflict, which has included Iranian missile fire targeting Gulf oil exporters.International security, defence cooperation on agenda"International security issues will be on the agenda," the Turkish foreign ministry source said.The discussions are expected to cover efforts to enhance defence capabilities, improve interoperability among the three countries' armed forces and deepen cooperation in the defence industry, including joint production and development, the source said.The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against acts of aggression.It stipulates that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be regarded as an attack on all three, a principle similar to Nato's Article 5 collective defence clause.Pact signed amid regional conflictThe three countries share concerns over the military positions of Israel and Iran as the wider region remains affected by conflict.Six months after the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran, negotiations remain at an impasse, while President Donald Trump's administration has stepped up financial pressure on Tehran.The Mecca agreement was signed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.The pact seeks to strengthen defence cooperation and collective deterrence among the three countries, though it does not specify detailed operational or military commitments.Alliance open to expansionTurkey, which has Nato's second-largest military, has said the agreement with nuclear-armed Pakistan and Saudi Arabia is open to expansion and does not seek to replace existing alliances.Egypt has been identified as a potential candidate.Bangladesh could also consider joining the pact, Reuters reported earlier, citing junior foreign minister Humayun Kabir.A Bangladesh foreign ministry source told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had invited Dhaka to join the agreement, though no timeline for the invitation was provided.Iran, meanwhile, has said it has not received an invitation to join the Mecca Pact, although proposals had been made for discussions with the three countries on regional security issues.

articles.title: Wind turbine blades are built to survive decades and are difficult to recycle; an Iowa plant mechanically shreds them into fibres and powders for concrete, mortar and asphalt
articles.summary: US News: Wind turbine blades can last for years, but what happens to them after they are no longer needed is a challenge. A facility in Fairfax, Iowa, USA, is .
articles.body: Wind turbine blades can last for years, but what happens to them after they are no longer needed is a challenge. A facility in Fairfax, Iowa, USA, is now recycling old wind turbine blades and turning their materials into products that can be used in concrete, mortar and asphalt.Regen Fiber opened its production facility in Fairfax in 2024 and began production at the site. The company has developed an all-mechanical recycling process for wind turbine blades. According to Recycling Today, unlike processes that use heat or chemicals, this method relies on mechanical processing to break the blades down.The recycled materials can be used in industrial applications, including the production of concrete, mortar and asphalt. The process is designed to recover materials from the blades and prepare them for use in construction projects, including projects linked to the energy industry.The facility is expected to process more than 30,000 tons of wind turbine blades each year when operating on a one-shift-per-day schedule.How blades are processedThe recycling process begins with extracting reusable components from the blades. The blades are then mechanically shredded. During this process, materials including fiberglass mesh and polyester resins are prepared for use in concrete and asphalt production. The company describes the method as an “all-mechanical recycling process” that avoids using heat or chemicals.The shredded blade materials are converted into fibres and additives. These materials are intended for use by concrete and asphalt producers. According to the recyclers, its process recycles 100 per cent of the wind turbine blade.Jeff Woods, director of business development at Travero, which owns the company, said the recycled materials can also help improve the performance of concrete and asphalt.“Our process recycles 100 percent of the wind turbine blade, creating fibers and additives that enhance the durability and environmental resistance of concrete and asphalt,” Woods said.He added that the materials can improve the structural integrity of roads and buildings and make them more resilient.The process therefore gives the recovered blade materials another use instead of treating them simply as waste.30,000 tons of blades a yearThe Fairfax facility is Rthe company's main production site and is located at its headquarters. At full one-shift production, the facility is expected to process more than 30,000 tons of blades annually.The Fairfax facility is not the company’s only operation connected to wind turbine blade recycling. There is also a facility in Des Moines, Iowa, that handles new turbine blade manufacturing scrap material.The company also operates a blade processing facility in Lubbock, Texas. That facility is located to handle end-of-life blades from the southwestern United States, an area with significant wind power activity.The different facilities handle different types of blade material. The Des Moines operation focuses on scrap generated during the manufacture of new turbine blades, while Fairfax and Lubbock are connected to the processing of end-of-life blades.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iran war creates two front defence dilemma for US against China and Russia
articles.summary: International News: The US war with Iran is creating a military dilemma that extends far beyond the Middle East, with the heavy use of American missiles and air-defence i.
articles.body: The US war with Iran is creating a military dilemma that extends far beyond the Middle East, with the heavy use of American missiles and air-defence interceptors raising concerns over Washington’s ability to deter or respond to potential threats from China and Russia.US military planners are increasingly worried that weapons consumed or shifted to the Middle East have left critical gaps in America’s wider global defence posture.The shortages are particularly acute in Europe, where US inventories of PAC-3 Patriot air-defence interceptors and ATACMS surface-to-surface missiles have fallen to what officials described as “beyond critical” levels.Other weapons, including precision-strike missiles, guided rockets and THAAD interceptors, have also been drawn down or moved from Europe to the Middle East, forcing the US European Command to adjust its operational plans.The Wall Street Journal reported, citing US officials, that by mid-July the US had expended about 1,700 Patriot air-defence interceptors and more than 200 THAAD antimissile interceptors, while US Navy ships had fired another 150 Standard Missile interceptors against Iranian missiles and drones. Iran, meanwhile, had fired more than 1,500 ballistic missiles and 6,000 large drones during the war.The depletion is not limited to weapons already used in combat. The US has also moved air-defence units from Europe and the Pacific to the Middle East to protect American forces and key infrastructure from Iranian attacks. These deployments have been extended, placing additional strain on the Pentagon’s ability to respond quickly to a future crisis elsewhere.The implications are particularly significant for Taiwan. The shrinking inventories have increasingly led US administration officials to assess that Washington may not be able to fully execute its existing contingency plans to defend Taiwan against a Chinese invasion if such a crisis were to occur in the near term, according to The Wall Street Journal report.The strain is also complicating the US military’s ability to support Ukraine. Western stocks of air-defence interceptors are already under pressure, limiting the ability to provide additional systems to Kyiv as Russia continues missile attacks. At the same time, US allies are facing delays in receiving munitions they have purchased from Washington, adding to concerns about the broader capacity of the Western defence-industrial base.The pressure is also exposing a problem with replacing advanced weapons. The Wall Street Journal reported that rebuilding stocks moved from Japan, South Korea and Germany could take years, potentially leaving gaps in US military readiness.

articles.title: US mother pleads guilty to killing 11-month-old son to keep him from his father, says it was 'worth it'
articles.summary: US News: A New Mexico woman, Madeline Veronique Daly, has pleaded guilty to murdering her 11-month-old son to keep him away from his father, expressing that the act was 'worth it'. The tragic case raises questions about custody disputes and parental rights.
articles.body: A US mother who kidnapped her 11-month-old son and fatally shot him inside an RV in New Mexico has pleaded guilty to first-degree murder after telling investigators she believed killing the child was “worth it” to prevent his father from getting custody, Cowboy State Daily reported.Madeline Veronique Daly, 36, took her son, Basil Stoner, from Wyoming to New Mexico despite a court order that had granted emergency custody to the boy’s father.The Grant County Sheriff’s Office found Daly at an RV park near Silver City on December 23 after she applied for a local job. When officers arrived, Daly ran into an RV, and deputies surrounded the vehicle.Officers then heard a single gunshot. They entered the RV and found Basil had been shot in the face with a 9mm handgun. Daly also attempted to turn the weapon on herself, but officers restrained her, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by the outlet.The shooting happened as police closed in on Daly after she had taken the child across state lines in breach of the custody order. Basil’s father had told investigators that he last saw his son on September 28.During interrogation, Daly said she had taken Basil because she did not want him travelling between Nebraska and Wyoming twice a month.As per the affidavit, she said she “was not going to allow her (then) 8-month-old baby go back and forth from Nebraska to Wyoming twice a month”.Investigators asked Daly what she was thinking when she saw law enforcement approaching the RV. She replied: “Jake can’t get Basil.”Daly also told police she believed she was keeping her son “safe”. She said killing him was “worth it” if it meant his father and other paternal relatives would never have the opportunity to see him.She made further claims that Basil “would have been in danger and molested” if she had left the trailer with him. She also alleged that his father had never wanted anything to do with the child “financially, physically, emotionally ever”.Authorities have not substantiated those claims.Daly pleaded guilty to first-degree murder on Wednesday, prosecutors said. She now faces a maximum sentence of life in prison.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: NHS pension system declared a retired worker dead and stopped paying her; she borrowed money to fly to Britain to prove she was alive
articles.summary: UK News: A retired NHS worker living in Cape Town found herself in an extraordinary financial crisis after the organisation responsible for her pension payment.
articles.body: A retired NHS worker living in Cape Town found herself in an extraordinary financial crisis after the organisation responsible for her pension payments mistakenly recorded her as dead. Her pension stopped arriving in May 2026, leaving her struggling to pay everyday bills and forcing her to borrow money simply to travel to Britain and try to prove that she was still alive. The woman, who worked for the NHS for 11 years before retiring to South Africa in 2015, said repeated phone calls and emails failed to resolve the problem. Her situation became even more difficult because she was already dealing with financial hardship after a similar pension problem the previous year.NHS pension payments stopped after she was wrongly recorded as deadThe pensioner first discovered something was wrong when her NHS pension stopped arriving in May. When she contacted the NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA), which administers the NHS pension scheme, she was reportedly told that its records showed she was deceased. Instead of receiving a straightforward explanation or having the error quickly corrected, she said her attempts to contact the organisation repeatedly led nowhere. Her emails received automated responses, while calls did not produce a solution. The interruption was particularly serious because the pension was an important source of income for her and her husband. The couple were already under severe financial pressure and were worried about meeting their regular bills. The pensioner also said she could no longer afford the cost of making international calls to the NHSBSA. Her financial difficulties had become so severe that she had even been unable to pay for dental treatment for a broken tooth.Retired NHS worker borrowed money to fly to Britain and prove she was aliveWith the problem still unresolved, the woman travelled from Cape Town to the UK using money borrowed from a friend. She hoped that appearing in person would finally persuade the pension authority that she was alive. Instead, her trip did not immediately solve the problem. After arriving in Britain, she was told that an NHSBSA system upgrade meant the organisation could only deal with general enquiries for several days. She was subsequently informed that her case required an investigation and that she could have to wait up to 30 days for a response. The pensioner was left in Britain for longer than expected, staying on a friend's sofa while attempting to resolve the matter. Her elderly husband remained in South Africa.This was not the first time her NHS pension had been disruptedThe mistaken death record came after another pension problem had already caused serious difficulties for the retired NHS worker. In December 2025, her pension payments were also interrupted after someone apparently changed her account details and the money was paid to another person. She was eventually able to resolve that issue by providing identity verification, but she said she went without her pension for four months and had to borrow money from her brother during that period. The second disruption therefore came after months of financial uncertainty, making the latest mistake particularly damaging. This time, however, the problem was not an incorrect bank account. The pension authority's records had apparently linked her to a death record, effectively treating her as someone who had died.NHSBSA admits an error was made in its recordsThe case was eventually escalated after The Guardian became involved. Three weeks after the newspaper contacted NHSBSA, the organisation paid three months of outstanding pension payments into the woman's account. NHSBSA also apologised for the distress and financial hardship caused by the mistake. A spokesperson said an error had been made in the records and that it had now been corrected. The organisation added that it took its responsibility to pension scheme members seriously and that the case had demonstrated areas where it needed to improve. NHSBSA also said it would discuss compensation with the pensioner, including the expenses she had incurred as a result of the ordeal.Why a pensioner being wrongly declared dead can cause serious problemsFor someone dependent on a pension for regular income, having payments suddenly stopped can quickly turn an administrative error into a financial crisis. In this case, the consequences extended far beyond a missing monthly payment. The pensioner struggled with everyday expenses, could not afford international calls to resolve the issue and ultimately borrowed money to travel thousands of miles to Britain. The episode also raises questions about how pension administrators verify information before stopping someone's income. A mistake in a database may appear minor on paper, but for the person affected, it can mean unpaid bills, debt and considerable emotional distress. The NHSBSA has now corrected the woman's records and restored the missed payments, but the pensioner is still seeking compensation for the costs and hardship caused by the error. The case highlights how a seemingly simple administrative mistake can have consequences that reach far beyond the computer system where it began.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In one Nepal district, flood catastrophe is measured in bodies and burial trenches
articles.summary: The devastating flash floods in the Himalayan region swept so many people downstream that authorities in one Nepalese district have begun burying bodies in t...
articles.body:
KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — The devastating flash floods in the Himalayan region swept so many people downstream that authorities in one Nepalese district have begun burying bodies in temporary graves before they can be identified, prompting accusations that Hindu funeral traditions are being ignored.

In south-central Nepal's Chitwan district, the scale of the catastrophe was evident in some 250 bodies awaiting identification and the hastily dug trenches for their temporary burial following Wednesday's catastrophic floods and mudslides , which killed at least 800 people and left more than 3,000 missing in Nepal and Tibet.

The bodies were carried hundreds of kilometers downstream by the Bhotekoshi River from the flood's epicenter before being recovered in Chitwan.

Authorities carried out a temporary burial of about 100 victims on Saturday, officials said, as forensic teams struggled to cope. A convoy of vehicles carrying bodies entered a lush, forested area as an excavator dug a wide trench in the red earth while officials and media looked on.

Anil Thapa, a police inspector coordinating the handling of the bodies, said another 50 bodies were having DNA samples taken ahead of their likely burial Sunday.

Authorities preserve the DNA samples, photograph distinguishing facial features and record other identifying details, Thapa said. The bodies are assigned a reference number to help families claim them later.

Thapa said many of the bodies had remained submerged in floodwaters for about four days and were already decomposing by the time they were recovered.

Across the region, homes, vehicles and farm tractors still lay partially buried in mud.

Limited forensic infrastructure and inadequate morgue capacity in the district further strained efforts to manage the overwhelming number of bodies recovered from the disaster, officials said.

High humidity and sweltering heat accelerated decomposition, compounding the challenges as health experts warned that leaving the remains exposed could increase the risk of disease.

Fresh landslides in the area on Sunday closed the main highway linking the capital city of Kathmandu and Chitwan, a day after it partially reopened, complicating efforts to move bodies and relief supplies.

As survivors grappled with the aftermath, criticism of the burials mounted. Some residents said the dead had waited days for their last rites and were denied dignity in death. Families still waiting to locate missing relatives and some public figures questioned whether authorities moved too quickly.

The issue is particularly sensitive in Nepal, a predominantly Hindu nation where the dead are traditionally cremated.

Ruby Chaudhary, who has two missing relatives, said the burials should not proceed without families' consent.

"The dead deserve to be treated with dignity," she said. "Our tradition is to cremate them on the riverbank, surrounded by their immediate family."

A former prime minister, Baburam Bhattarai, said it was inappropriate to dispose of unidentified bodies before search and rescue operations were complete and without broader consultation with families of the missing.

If morgues were insufficient, authorities could have mobilized emergency resources to set up temporary morgues or secure cold storage facilities, he said in a social media post Saturday night.

Officials said the burials were a temporary measure necessitated by health concerns and limited capacity.

"People are worried that this could be a permanent burial, but it is only temporary management," Thapa said. "If someone is able to verify the identity later using the available information, they can take back the body and perform the appropriate funeral rites."

Amrit Bahadur Rai, Nepal's foreign secretary, said the temporary burial of unidentified bodies was carried out in line with internationally accepted disaster-management protocols, including those of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

"Families can match records later, and will be allowed to exhume (the remains later) for necessary rituals," Rai said at a press briefing in Kathmandu.

articles.title: German police hunt for prisoner after daring rooftop escape
articles.summary: Duisburg, Germany (dpa) -A 35-year-old prisoner staged a dramatic escape from a jail in western Germany early on Sunday, apparently scaling the outside of th...
articles.body:
Duisburg, Germany (dpa) -A 35-year-old prisoner staged a dramatic escape from a jail in western Germany early on Sunday, apparently scaling the outside of the building before fleeing across the roof.

The man escaped from Duisburg-Hamborn prison at around 3:20 am (0120 GMT), the Justice Ministry of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia said.

He remained at large on Sunday afternoon, with authorities saying there was still no trace of him.

Investigators have since discovered that the prisoner had created a hiding place beneath the linoleum floor of his cell that had apparently gone unnoticed during cell inspections, a ministry spokesman said.

No tools were found in the concealed space.

Authorities believe the man sawed through a bar covering the window of his third-floor cell, which faced an inner courtyard. He then used his cell table as a lever to force open a second, finer security grille covering the window.

The prisoner squeezed through the narrow opening and apparently climbed the facade on the courtyard side of the building to reach the roof. He then made his way down the outside of the prison by means that remain unclear, the spokesman said.

"Today's escape is absolutely unacceptable. The top priority now is the swift apprehension of the fugitive remand prisoner," North Rhine-Westphalia Justice Minister Benjamin Limbach said.

"We will fully establish how this security breach was possible so that the necessary consequences can be taken immediately based on the findings," Limbach said.

The man had been remanded in custody on suspicion of theft since February 10. At the end of May, he was sentenced to six years in prison for two residential burglaries involving substantial losses, although the verdict is not yet legally binding.

According to information from judicial sources, he is accused of stealing valuable jewellery as well as more than €200,000 in cash.
