articles.title: A West Texas rancher rejected wind turbines twice before agreeing to 7 on his family ranch; the royalties now help pay for feed and workers and keep the operation running
articles.summary: US News: A fifth-generation West Texas rancher twice rejected plans to put wind turbines on his family’s property before eventually agreeing to host seven turb.
articles.body: A fifth-generation West Texas rancher twice rejected plans to put wind turbines on his family’s property before eventually agreeing to host seven turbines. Today, the wind project has become an important source of regular income for John E Davis, helping him continue his ranching operation and invest in other projects in the community.Davis, a former Texas state representative and former chair of the House Economic and Small Business Development Committee, owns the ranch with his brother, Keith Davis. The property is near the Concho County-Menard County line. The family was first approached about the wind project in 2016, but Davis said they did not want “any of those ugly old wind turbines” on their land, Texas Energy and Power.com reported.The developers returned about a year and a half later. The brothers rejected the proposal again before eventually agreeing to join the Cactus Flats wind project in Concho County. Developed by RES, the Cactus Flats Wind Facility has a capacity of 148 MW and includes 43 turbines. Seven of them are now on the Davis family property.The turbines began going up in 2018 and started generating income for the ranch in 2019. Davis said the regular payments have helped him continue operating the ranch. He also described the wind revenue as “a lifeline for us”.Why Davis changed his mindThe decision eventually came down to the need for a stable source of income from the ranch. Davis said his brother negotiated a contract that included minimum royalty payments, with the payments adjusted upwards every five years.The family also discussed the proposal with Davis’s father, who had worked for Shell Oil and was involved in land and right-of-way work. Davis recalled that his father asked, “Well, does it pay any money?” When Davis told him that it did, his father agreed to the idea.The wind payments became important as the ranch dealt with changing livestock prices, drought and rising feed costs. Davis raises sheep, goats and cattle, including Wagyu cattle, Rambouillet sheep and Angora goats.The regular income helps pay for ranch workers, animal feed, fences, water equipment and repairs. While livestock income can rise and fall with market conditions, the wind lease provides a more predictable source of money.Davis also recalled what happened when the first payment arrived. His wife, Jane, received half of the income because they were married. She initially offered the cheque back because the land had come from Davis’s family. Davis told her, “give to Jane Davis what is Jane Davis’s.”He said she now receives an automatic payment every three months. Her response, he recalled, is, “Thank you very much” and “John, keep ranching.”Ranching continues under the turbinesThe wind project did not replace the family’s ranching operation. Davis continues to raise animals on the property, including about 200 nanny goats, 200 Dorper ewes and around 30 cows.The project also improved access around the ranch. Davis said travelling from the entrance to the top of the property once took about 25 minutes because of the rocky ground. After roads were built for the turbines, he said the same journey takes about three and a half minutes.The turbines have also become part of everyday life for the animals. During summer, Davis said sheep can be seen resting in the shade cast by the turbines.Davis rejected claims that the turbines had made the property unsuitable for hunting or livestock. He said his hunting income had not been affected and that he had not seen dead birds around the turbines.The turbine income has also given Davis financial flexibility to invest in another project in Menard, Texas. He developed a two-acre site on a former Exxon property into what he calls the Menard station. The site includes an EV charging station, livestock, a music stage, a farm stand and a book exchange.The site also sells products such as farm eggs and is being developed to include a beer garden and Wagyu beef products. Davis said he plans to sell Wagyu franks and bratwurst and hold live music events.A question of rural property rightsDavis, who identifies as a conservative Republican, said landowners should be able to decide whether to host wind, solar or other energy infrastructure on their property.He argued that renewable energy should not automatically be treated as a political issue. In his view, using wind and sunlight available on rural land can give landowners another way to keep their operations running.He said opposition to renewable energy can hurt rural landowners who depend on different income sources to maintain working ranches.Davis described the issue as one of private property rights. “It’s private property rights. It’s our land. It’s mine. It’s a way to get grit, to use the land to support your family, support your next generation,” he said.He also argued that energy development can benefit rural communities through roads, tax revenue and other economic activity.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Rebuilt with India aid, flood-erased Nepal school seeks help to rebuild on higher ground
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT, NEPAL): Three warnings came within minutes the day it flooded, an accountant rushed in saying water was gushing in, a teache.
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT, NEPAL): Three warnings came within minutes the day it flooded, an accountant rushed in saying water was gushing in, a teacher relayed a phone call from upstream saying the area had been “swallowed”, and a parent arrived on a scooter to take his daughter away.Principal Rajendra Dawadi immediately ordered around 900 students at Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School out. They escaped before the river wiped out the 76-year-old campus. Now, Dawadi, teachers and students agree on one thing: classes must restart at the earliest, but the school must never be rebuilt beside the river. It has to rise on higher ground.“The children -- even some of our teachers and domestic staff -- are scared of the river.... it is a snaking ghost,” Dawadi, 47, told TOI on Sunday. “When they look at it, they feel afraid.”Close to a thousand people, including the children, had been inside the school when the warnings arrived. Thirty girls were in the residential hostel. When they asked Dawadi where they could go because their homes were far away, he told them to follow him uphill.Dawadi ordered a non-teaching employee to ring the bell and teachers began clearing classrooms. Staff helped students suffering panic attacks. One girl was being examined by a nurse in the infirmary. All students who were inside the school survived.Two staff members remain missing, Dawadi said. Non-teaching employee Chulrim Lama had been behind him during the evacuation and may have turned back towards the school, possibly to close a door. Lower-secondary teacher Santos Parihar was believed to have been in his room in the teachers’ quarters.Tribhuvan Trishuli, the oldest school across the flood-hit Rasuwa, Dhading and Nuwakot districts, had 1,643 students. The flood destroyed virtually everything it owned, including an 18-room, three-storey block constructed with assistance from the Embassy of India after the 2015 earthquake. All that remained of the school’s property were two buses. One of them had been provided by the Embassy of India.“Everything is washed away by the flood,” Dawadi said. “Previously, at the time of many disasters, Indian govt helped us. We are also hopeful this time that the Indian govt will help us re-establish our school.”Dawadi said India’s association with the school went back to before the 2015 earthquake. The proposal for the 18-room building had already been accepted before the quake, and the three-storey block was subsequently constructed with the embassy's assistance.Students described the terror of watching their school disappear.“We were getting ready for the morning assembly when teachers started screaming for us to run up the hill. I left my backpack and books behind in the classroom. Looking back down from the ridge and seeing the river wash over our playground was terrifying, but I am just glad all my friends made it safely,” Class 10 student Sunita Tamang told TOI.Class 12 student Rohan Shrestha remembered hearing the flood before seeing it. “The roar of the river sounded like a low thunder before we even saw the mud coming. The teachers moved fast getting everyone out of the hostels and to higher ground. The school is completely covered in mud now, and we don't know when we can go back to class, but we are looking after each other in the temporary camp,” he said.For Dawadi, restarting classes quickly was as much about restoring a sense of normalcy as education. “The children needed to see their friends and teachers again and return to some routine after the trauma,” he said.A large room in a private house, rented premises, a banquet hall or a govt building could serve as a temporary school. The municipality could also help establish a temporary learning centre, teachers hoped. Dawadi’s only non-negotiable condition was that it had to be on higher ground. “In a safe area, we will start the temporary school or temporary learning centre,” he said. “If possible, we will take rented houses and think about how to continue their learning.”Connectivity, however, remained the immediate hurdle. Dawadi said around 65-70% of the school’s students lived on one side of Trishuli river and 30-35% on the other. Others depended on buses, rented rooms near the school or its residential hostel. With river crossings destroyed, children who had studied together until Wednesday were now separated by Trishuli. “Connectivity is more important. If a Bailey bridge is established here, then we can restart very soon,” Dawadi said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2005, a couple bought a 2,300-acre Napa ranch for $8 million; after a 17-year battle over plans for vineyards, the land was bought for $24 million and is becoming a public preserve
articles.summary: US News: For years the fate of a large swath of Napa Valley wilderness has been tied up in competing visions: neat rows of vineyards or a continuous landscape .
articles.body: For years the fate of a large swath of Napa Valley wilderness has been tied up in competing visions: neat rows of vineyards or a continuous landscape for wildlife to roam. Now, after a long legal and environmental fight, the 2,300-acre property is headed for a very different future: a public nature preserve. The former Walt Ranch is now the Osos Ridge Preserve, a nod to the black bears that regularly roam the rugged landscape. The Land Trust of Napa County bought the property in 2023 for $24 million, and will forever safeguard it and make it available to the public in spring 2027, states the Napal and Trust website.Vineyard to conservation planThe property, along the Atlas Peak ridgeline in the eastern hills of Napa County, was the focus of a years-long fight over plans to develop commercial vineyards. The land was bought in 2005 by vintners Craig and Kathryn Hall for $8 million. Later plans to develop vineyards met opposition over possible impacts to old-growth trees, wildlife habitat and watersheds. The property was the subject of controversy for years until the Land Trust acquired it in 2023, protecting the landscape from the proposed development. Grants from the State Coastal Conservancy, the Wildlife Conservation Board and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation paid for the purchase. The Halls also gave $6 million toward the purchase.Napa wildlife highwayAccording to the report, Osos Ridge Preserve is not just a large undeveloped tract. It’s an important wildlife corridor, running unbroken from Foss Valley to Howell Mountain. Mountain lions, bobcats and black-tailed deer use the landscape, while black bears are particularly prominent. The preserve's new name was inspired by the Spanish word for bears, osos. Wildlife needs safe pathways to escape danger during wildfires, and later to return to their habitat, making the property particularly valuable. Conservationists say the preserve is an important refuge and corridor for animals across the region.Ancient landscapes and uncommon plantsThe preserve’s ecological value isn’t just in its larger animals. It boasts 2,300 acres of oak woodlands, intact grasslands and sensitive vernal pools. These diverse habitats support rare and endangered plants including Redwood Lily, Napa Bluecurls, Jepson’s Leptosiphon and Narrow-anthered brodiaea. The property had the highest biodiversity ranking in California’s Areas of Conservation Emphasis program, due to the concentration of sensitive species.The preserve also includes key watersheds for the Napa River and Putah Creek and Lake Berryessa. The area is traversed by Capell Creek and Milliken Creek, the latter a significant source of municipal water for Napa. Also, the area's history stretches back even further. Archaeological evidence indicates that Indigenous communities, including the Miwok, Patwin and Wappo peoples, used parts of the landscape as seasonal camps.A sanctuary for people and wildlifeToday the property is dedicated to conservation and restoration, but it also has a future as a place for the public. The Land Trust will partner with the Napa County Regional Park and Open Space District to manage the preserve. Plans are in place for trails, educational infrastructure and visitor access, with a public opening planned for spring 2027.Image Courtesy: Napal and TrustCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iranian woman sentenced to death for filming burning store during January protests
articles.summary: Middle East News: Leila Abolhasani, a 43-year-old Iranian woman, has been sentenced to death for capturing images of arson during January protests, raising concerns about the suppression of dissent in Iran and the international response to such measures.
articles.body: An Iranian woman has been sentenced to death by hanging after she was accused of involvement in the arson of a grocery store she had photographed during anti-government protests in January.Leila Abolhasani, 43, mother of two, was arrested on January 8 in Shahin Shahr, a satellite city in Iran's central Isfahan province, after taking pictures of a fire at an Ofogh Koorosh supermarket, a major discount grocery chain. She has since been held at Dowlatabad Prison in Isfahan, Iranwire reported.Abolhasani was convicted under the charge of “Moharebeh”, a term commonly translated as “enmity against God” or “waging war against God”. The charge can carry the death penalty under Iran's Islamic legal system.A source told IranWire that authorities accused Abolhasani of being involved in setting the store on fire. However, details of the evidence allegedly linking her to the blaze, the proceedings during her trial and the nature of her legal defence have not been made public.In late May, Vahid Hemmatnejad, the presiding judge of Branch 5 of the Isfahan Revolutionary Court, sentenced Abolhasani to death by hanging.She appealed against the ruling and her case was subsequently transferred to Iran's Supreme Court, where the verdict is reportedly being reviewed.The case has emerged amid continuing international concern over the treatment of people arrested during Iran's January protests. The demonstrations resulted in a large-scale crackdown, with estimates of arrests and deaths varying between sources.An Iranian refugee who spoke to NewsNation (US based news outlet) described Abolhasani's case as a warning to others who document events or oppose the government.“She was arrested for documenting what was happening and was sentenced to death,” the refugee said.They argued that footage of the burning store could have drawn international attention to the government's response to the protests.“Her work could have been very effective in showing the world how brutal and savage the regime is, and they do not want the world to see the truth,” the refugee said.The refugee added that authorities wanted Abolhasani's case to become “a lesson to anyone who tries to speak the truth about the regime” and said the case was intended to create fear among people who might otherwise consider documenting or exposing events.“They want people to remain silent and to keep the truth hidden forever,” the refugee said.The potential execution comes as Iran continues to face scrutiny over its use of the death penalty in cases involving national security charges.United Nations human rights chief Volker Türk said earlier this month that Iran had executed at least 56 people on national security-related charges since March 19. Of those cases, 27 were linked to the January protests.Türk also said executions and death sentences had increased since March, with more than 100 other people facing charges that could result in the death penalty.“The death penalty is incompatible with the right to life and irreconcilable with human dignity,” Türk said. “Such punishment has no place in our world.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump promises to ‘fill up’ SPR after US-Venezuela oil deal
articles.summary: President Trump said Sunday the U.S. will “fill up” the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) as a result of the oil deal his administration reached with the Venezuelan government. “One of the things I am going to do with the Venezuelan Oil is fill up the Strategic National Reserves,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding the…
articles.body:
President Trump said Sunday the U.S. will “fill up” the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) as a result of the oil deal his administration reached with the Venezuelan government.

“One of the things I am going to do with the Venezuelan Oil is fill up the Strategic National Reserves,” Trump wrote on Truth Social , adding the SPR was “virtually emptied” under former President Biden.

“The ‘topping out’ process will begin very shortly, and is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States,” the president added.

Trump said Friday his administration reached a deal with the Venezuelan government to grant the U.S. control of more than 65 billion barrels of oil from the South American country.

Sixty-five billion barrels account for roughly 21 percent of Venezuela’s total proven reserves of roughly 303 billion barrels as of 2023.

Under the deal, Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez granted a private company — a joint venture between the U.S. government and a private operator — 100-year “concessions” for oil fields containing 63 billion barrels of proven reserves, a U.S. official told The Hill.

The official did not name the private operator, but noted the U.S. government will have more than half of the new oil company’s value and will receive 55 percent “effective output” of the joint venture.

The deal, which multiple Democratic lawmakers have criticized , comes after U.S. forces captured former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January.

Rodriguez, who succeeded Maduro as president, said Friday the deal will lead to the development of 17 strategic fields and in excess of $209 billion in tax revenue generated for her government.

“These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernization of our industry, but also to our country’s economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere, and greater balance in international markets,” Rodriguez said in a statement .

In the week ending Aug. 21, the SPR had more than 289.7 million barrels of oil, down nearly 30 percent from the start of this year, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).

During Biden’s term, the amount in the SPR fell from 638 million-plus barrels in January 2021 to less than 395 million barrels in January 2025, per the EIA.

The authorized storage capacity of the SPR is 714 million barrels, according to the Energy Department .
